topic: Direct empirical methods for cross-version multimodal document element lineage and hierarchical provenance, with special attention to revised workbook provenance and message referring-expression grounding into versioned pages, regions, and cells.
executive_summary: Across the distinct studies represented here, document understanding improves when models retain spatial, hierarchical, table, and multimodal structure rather than relying only on flattened text. Evidence localization is repeatedly shown to be separable from answer correctness, and long-document results show that page and region routing become harder as scope and cross-page composition increase. Spreadsheet studies demonstrate useful within-workbook cell, formula, sheet, and structural provenance, while versioning studies demonstrate complementary mechanisms for persistent identity, similarity-based version recovery, and cross-version element alignment. However, these components have not been jointly validated for revised workplace attachments. Likewise, referring-expression grounding is empirically demonstrated in GUI, scene-text, and visually grounded dialogue domains, but not directly for workplace messages pointing into versioned attachments, screenshots, pages, table rows, or spreadsheet cells.
themes: Spatial, hierarchical, and multimodal structure materially affects document and table understanding.
Answer correctness and evidence-grounding correctness are distinct evaluation dimensions.
Long-document understanding benefits from hierarchical evidence acquisition at page and region granularity.
Table understanding depends on recovering cell geometry, spanning relationships, hierarchy, and content rather than OCR text alone.
Spreadsheet reasoning benefits from multi-granular structural representations and explicit within-workbook provenance, while full-workbook task completion remains difficult.
Cross-version identity and differencing are addressed through persistent identifiers, semantic matching, similarity grouping, and element alignment in different domains.
Referring-expression grounding is empirically supported in GUI, scene-text, and situated-dialogue domains but not directly in workplace attachment-reference settings.
Existing provenance schemes cover different levels such as source tuple, page, region, answer span, sheet, and cell, but no admitted study validates their complete cross-version combination.

findings.statement: Across document and table benchmarks, explicitly representing spatial or hierarchical structure improves measured understanding relative to weaker structure-aware or text-only variants in the reported experiments.

Document-QA experiments show that answer correctness and evidence localization are not equivalent: models can answer correctly from the wrong page, localize the correct visual evidence but still reason incorrectly, or achieve substantially higher answer scores than strict attributed-answer scores.

On long-document benchmarks, evidence acquisition becomes harder with document length and distributed evidence, while hierarchical or coarse-to-fine page and region selection improves reported QA performance over the corresponding weaker retrieval or routing variants.

Table-recognition studies demonstrate recovery of structured cells, including spanning, empty, and hierarchical relationships, with large benchmark gains over comparison systems in several evaluated datasets; table-QA studies additionally tie answers to selected cells or recovered table hierarchy.

Spreadsheet experiments show that multi-granular retrieval, explicit structural representations, and verification improve measured spreadsheet-question performance, while workflow-level benchmarks still report much lower complete-task accuracy than cell-level modification accuracy.

Cross-version studies demonstrate several distinct mechanisms for lineage: persistent node identifiers can preserve logical XML-node identity across snapshots, semantic or structural matching can recover correspondence when explicit identity is unavailable, scientific-document alignment can match heterogeneous elements across revised PDFs, and spreadsheet similarity clustering can recover candidate version groups when version history is missing.

In adjacent grounding domains, explicit scene-text, dialogue-reference, spatial, or low-level referring supervision improves grounding of ambiguous referring expressions or screen objects in the reported datasets, including pronouns, omitted references, scene-text-dependent expressions, and GUI elements.

Several document-QA systems and benchmarks preserve inspectable hierarchical provenance within a document, including page identifiers, element or region locations, bounding boxes or masks, and in some cases explicit links from generated answer spans to supporting regions.

Flattening visually rich documents to OCR or plain text can lose useful evidence: long-document evaluations report weaknesses on chart- and image-dependent questions, structure-preserving table parsing improves downstream QA, and detailed visual descriptions outperform OCR-only evidence in an evaluated multimodal RAG comparison.

Provenance research distinguishes the location from which a value originates from the evidence that explains why an output exists, while lineage systems separately demonstrate tracing output items back to source tuples; these results establish distinct provenance semantics rather than a single interchangeable provenance notion.

contradictions.topic: Whether explicit grounding supervision improves answer accuracy
contradictions.note: LAT reports simultaneous gains in answering and attribution, and CiteVQA oracle analyses show better answering when correct evidence is supplied, but RefChartQA shows that grounding instruction tuning improves some backbones while reducing answer accuracy for UniChart, ChartGemma, and some Qwen2.5-VL splits. The evidence therefore does not support a universal claim that adding grounding supervision increases answer accuracy.

contradictions.topic: OCR/text pipelines versus native multimodal processing
contradictions.note: MMLongBench-Doc reports that most evaluated LVLMs underperform LLM counterparts given OCR text, except for stronger proprietary vision models, while MMDocRAG finds detailed VLM-generated visual descriptions outperform OCR-only evidence and LongDocURL finds structure-preserving parsing materially better than plain PyMuPDF text. These results differ by model capability, modality, and parsing representation and should not be averaged into a single modality winner.

contradictions.topic: Direct coordinate generation versus language-mediated evidence attribution
contradictions.note: The coordinate-free attribution study finds substantially higher recall and lower hallucination when models quote evidence text and a separate parser maps it to regions, whereas M3Grounder and Ferret-UI demonstrate strong direct mask or box grounding with dedicated architectures and supervision. The studies use different tasks and training regimes, so they support competing interfaces under different conditions rather than one universally superior representation.

contradictions.topic: What counts as useful reading-order structure
contradictions.note: The handwritten-document study evaluates reading order against annotated ordering sequences and shows large gains over simple geometric ordering, while the LLM-relation study finds GPT-derived relations align poorly with adjacency-oriented human labels yet improve downstream document tasks. This is an evaluation-target conflict: agreement with conventional reading-order annotations and downstream usefulness are not equivalent objectives.

contradictions.topic: Whether one evidence location is uniquely correct
contradictions.note: MP-DocVQA page-selection analysis and RefChartQA manual checking both identify cases with multiple defensible evidence locations, whereas attribution benchmarks such as CiteVQA score against defined gold evidence sets. The contradiction is not that gold localization is useless, but that single-positive evidence annotations can underrepresent valid alternative support.

gaps.description: The corpus still does not establish a complete method for maintaining evidence provenance across successive workplace attachment revisions, including stable attachment identity, version-relative source locations, semantic changes between versions, and lineage from an older cited region to its later counterpart. Version-aware retrieval, scientific-PDF alignment, XML persistent identity, and spreadsheet-version clustering cover separate components, but their combination remains unvalidated.
gaps.suggested_query: "document version alignment" multimodal provenance region lineage semantic change revised document attachments

gaps.description: Direct grounding of workplace-message referring expressions such as "this screenshot", "the highlighted row", "numbers below", or "use attachment v2" into attachment objects, pages, cells, or regions remains unvalidated. Existing scene-text, GUI, and visually grounded dialogue studies provide adjacent-domain evidence only.
gaps.suggested_query: "referring expression grounding" document multimodal attachment table cell screenshot coreference email

gaps.description: Comprehensive spreadsheet understanding remains open for formulas, hidden rows and sheets, cross-sheet references, merged regions, formatting semantics, units, named ranges, and provenance across revised workbook versions. Current workbook studies address retrieval, structure reconstruction, verification, workflow completion, clone detection, dependency structure, and within-state cell provenance but not this complete set.
gaps.suggested_query: "spreadsheet understanding" workbook formulas hidden sheets named ranges merged cells cross-sheet provenance version

gaps.description: No admitted paper validates one end-to-end provenance representation that jointly identifies attachment version, page, document element, exact region or spreadsheet cell, and answer span. Different studies validate subsets of this hierarchy, and the complete cross-version combination remains untested.
gaps.suggested_query: "evidence provenance" document question answering version page region cell answer span multimodal grounding

gaps.description: End-to-end behavior when extraction or grounding is unsupported, incomplete, or wrong remains insufficiently exercised. The corpus includes unanswerable-question evaluation and parser, retrieval, OCR, localization, attribution, and grounding failure analyses, but not a complete engineering contract distinguishing genuine evidence absence from parser, OCR, layout, retrieval, or grounding failure.

Robustness of candidate extraction and structural-preservation pipelines on heterogeneous workplace-style documents remains an engineering gap. No admitted benchmark jointly exercises sparse tables, merged and hierarchical structures, OCR corruption, irregular reading order, embedded visual objects, scanned pages, and explicit extraction-completeness accounting.

Operational scaling remains open for long documents, large tables, and realistic workbooks. The corpus reports page-routing costs, evidence-graph overhead, parsing limits, workbook inspection failures, and change-detection trade-offs, but does not close the system-level latency, memory, and throughput question for the target workload.

The corpus lacks one evaluation that simultaneously measures semantic correctness, extraction completeness, exact provenance, unsupported-evidence handling, and preservation of tables, images, document hierarchy, and reading order on workplace-style attachments. Existing benchmarks and metrics evaluate overlapping subsets rather than the complete combination.

actionable_insights: Synthesis-derived recommendation: represent evidence addresses as typed, hierarchical objects rather than reducing every citation to a text span; retain distinct fields for attachment/version identity, page or sheet, element type, region or cell address, and answer-span linkage.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: treat cross-version element correspondence as a separate relation from within-version location. A cell or region address should identify where evidence exists in one version, while a lineage relation should state whether and how that element corresponds to another version.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: keep exact source artifacts and extracted structural representations side by side so later corrections can be traced back to the version and region from which an interpretation was derived.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: evaluate answer correctness and provenance correctness independently, and include cases where an answer is correct despite wrong evidence as well as cases where the evidence is correctly localized but the reasoning result is wrong.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: distinguish genuine no-evidence cases from extraction, OCR, layout, retrieval, grounding, and unsupported-format failures in the engineering status model instead of mapping all of them to an empty result.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: construct spreadsheet evaluation fixtures that separately exercise formulas, cross-sheet dependencies, hidden content, merged cells, formatting and units, named ranges, images, and revision lineage rather than assuming ordinary visible-cell QA covers these behaviors.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: use workplace-message-to-attachment referring expressions as their own evaluation surface, including version-selecting expressions, row and cell references, positional language, visual emphasis, and ambiguous references with multiple candidate regions.

Synthesis-derived recommendation: do not combine page routing, region grounding, spreadsheet cell provenance, and cross-version alignment into a claimed validated provenance design until the combination itself has been tested end to end.
confidence_summary: Confidence is high for several design principles supported repeatedly across distinct document, table, spreadsheet, provenance, and long-document studies: structure affects understanding; evidence localization is separable from answer correctness; hierarchical retrieval can improve long-document evidence acquisition; and explicit identifiers or alignment mechanisms can preserve correspondence within their evaluated versioning domains. Confidence is medium for transferring referring-expression methods into workplace email and attachment settings because the direct evidence comes from GUI, scene-text, situated-dialogue, and related visual-grounding domains rather than workplace messages. Confidence is low for any claim that the literature already validates a complete cross-version workplace-attachment provenance stack. The component mechanisms are individually evidenced, but the combination is not.
limitations: The supplied corpus contains 53 analysis records but 52 distinct studies because manual-1048d6caf2 and doi-10-1109-tmm-2022-3219642 describe the same Scene-Text Oriented Referring Expression Comprehension study; they were treated as one independent piece of evidence.
The synthesis was produced from reduced per-paper analyses rather than the full papers, so unreported methodological details, negative results, and dataset caveats may be absent.

The evidence spans heterogeneous domains including document QA, scientific PDFs, XML warehouses, business tables, general spreadsheets, GUI screenshots, charts, clinical guidelines, and situated dialogue; results from these domains are not direct production-email evidence.
Several strong results come from synthetic, benchmark, or adjacent-domain settings. They support mechanisms and experimental hypotheses but do not establish accuracy on workplace attachments.

Metrics are heterogeneous across papers, including ANLS, F1, IoU, TEDS, task accuracy, cell accuracy, retrieval accuracy, and attributed-answer metrics, so numerical results are not directly comparable across studies.
The corpus contains multiple components that could be combined into a hierarchical cross-version provenance representation, but no admitted study empirically validates that combined scheme.
The inherited handoffs from earlier Topics are treated only as project context and not as evidence for any finding or gap status in this synthesis.

gap_status.note: The new corpus adds direct scientific-PDF cross-version element alignment and existing XML persistent-identity and spreadsheet-version-recovery evidence, but no study combines stable attachment identity, version-relative locations, semantic change, and old-to-new region lineage for workplace attachments.

Grounding is demonstrated for GUI elements, scene-text objects, and situated-dialogue references, including pronouns and omitted references, but no admitted study evaluates workplace-message expressions grounded into versioned attachments, pages, rows, cells, or screenshots.

Spreadsheet studies now cover multi-granular retrieval, structural reconstruction, verification, formula-aware inspection, workflow execution, clone detection, and within-state provenance, but the complete inventory of hidden structures, formatting semantics, units, named ranges, and cross-revision provenance is not jointly evaluated.

CiteVQA, M3Grounder, long-document routing systems, and spreadsheet retrieval systems validate different provenance levels, but no admitted paper jointly validates attachment version, page, element, exact region or cell, and answer-span identity in one end-to-end representation.

The corpus contains partial failure analyses, unanswerable-question evaluation, attribution hallucination measurements, and parser or retrieval failure modes, but no complete engineering evaluation distinguishes genuine evidence absence from every major upstream failure class.

Individual studies cover difficult tables, distorted pages, reading order, multimodal documents, and scans, but no single admitted benchmark jointly covers the full heterogeneous workplace-style extraction and completeness surface.

The corpus reports scaling behavior and costs for individual long-document, graph, matching, differencing, and spreadsheet approaches, but no study provides target-workload system-level latency, memory, and throughput validation.

CiteVQA, SMuDGE, MMLongBench-Doc, LongDocURL, table-recognition benchmarks, and spreadsheet benchmarks measure overlapping subsets, but none simultaneously evaluates semantic correctness, extraction completeness, exact provenance, unsupported-evidence handling, multimodal preservation, hierarchy, and reading order.
